'''David William Masser''' {{post-nominals|country=GBR|FRS}} (born 8 November 1948) is [[professor emeritus]] in the Department of Mathematics and Computer Science at the [[University of Basel]].<ref name="Basel">{{cite web |url=https://dmi.unibas.ch/en/persons/david-masser/ |website=[[University of Basel]] |title=Prof. Dr. David Masser |access-date=5 March 2021}}</ref> He is known for his work in [[transcendental number theory]], [[Diophantine approximation]], and [[Diophantine geometry]]. With [[Joseph Oesterlé]] in 1985, Masser formulated the [[abc conjecture]], which has been called "the most important unsolved problem in [[Diophantine analysis]]".<ref name="Goldfeld">{{Citation |authorlink=Dorian Goldfeld |first=Dorian |last=Goldfeld |title=Beyond the last theorem |journal=The Sciences |date=March–April 1996 |volume=36 |issue=2 |pages=34–40 |doi=10.1002/j.2326-1951.1996.tb03243.x }}.</ref>

==Early life and education==
Masser was born on 8 November 1948 in London, England.<ref name="CV">{{cite web |url=https://dmi.unibas.ch/fileadmin/user_upload/dmi/Forschung/Mathematik/Zahlentheorie/CV_Masser_April20.pdf |title=Curriculum Vitae and Publication list of D. W. Masser |website=[[University of Basel]] |date=14 February 2020 |access-date=5 March 2021}}</ref> He graduated from [[Trinity College, Cambridge|Trinity College]], [[University of Cambridge|Cambridge]] with a B.A. (Hons) in 1970.<ref name="CV"/> In 1974, he obtained his M.A. and Ph.D. at the University of Cambridge,<ref name="CV"/> with a doctoral thesis under the supervision of [[Alan Baker (mathematician)|Alan Baker]] titled ''Elliptic Functions and Transcendence''.<ref name=mathgene>{{MathGenealogy |id=7915 }}</ref>

==Career==
Masser was a Lecturer at the [[University of Nottingham]] from 1973 to 1975, before spending the 1975–1976 year as a Research Fellow of Trinity College at the University of Cambridge.<ref name="CV"/> He returned to the University of Nottingham to serve as a Lecturer from 1976 to 1979 and then as a Reader from 1979 to 1983.<ref name="CV"/> He was a professor at the [[University of Michigan]] from 1983 to 1992.<ref name="CV"/> He then moved to the Mathematics Institute at the [[University of Basel]] and became emeritus there in 2014.<ref name="Basel"/><ref name="CV"/><ref name="IAS"/>

==Research==
Masser's research focuses on [[transcendental number theory]], [[Diophantine approximation]], and [[Diophantine geometry]].<ref name="IAS"/>  The ''abc'' conjecture originated as the outcome of attempts by Oesterlé and Masser to understand the [[Szpiro conjecture]] about [[elliptic curve]]s.<ref>{{citation|title=Arithmetic deformation theory via arithmetic fundamental groups and nonarchimedean theta functions, notes on the work of Shinichi Mochizuki|journal=European Journal of Mathematics|first=Ivan|last=Fesenko|volume=1|issue=3|pages=405–440|year=2015|url=https://www.maths.nottingham.ac.uk/personal/ibf/notesoniut.pdf|doi=10.1007/s40879-015-0066-0|s2cid=52085917|doi-access=free|access-date=5 March 2021|archive-date=15 June 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180615214843/https://www.maths.nottingham.ac.uk/personal/ibf/notesoniut.pdf|url-status=dead}}.</ref>

==Awards==
Masser was an [[invited speaker at the International Congress of Mathematicians]] in Warsaw in 1983.<ref name="CV"/><ref name="IAS">{{cite web |url=https://www.ias.edu/scholars/david-w-masser |website=[[Institute for Advanced Study]] |title=David W. Masser |date=9 December 2019 |access-date=5 March 2021}}</ref> In 1991, he received the [[Humboldt Prize]].<ref name="CV"/> He was elected as a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] in 2005.<ref name="CV"/><ref name="IAS"/> In 2014, he was elected as a Member of the [[Academia Europaea]].<ref name="CV"/><ref name="IAS"/>
